column1: Sociology|broad_field|idea|sociology|§1.1, What Are Society and Culture?; Studying Patterns|Connect everyday interactions with patterned relationships and institutions at larger social scales.|Q21201|Same systematic study of society and interaction as the baseline control.|

Social network|topic|idea|ties|Chapter 3 introduction; §3.1|Represent people and relationships to inspect how local connections shape access to wider social worlds.|Q2715623|Same sociological network concept; preserve registered identity.|

Weak ties|idea|idea|ties|§3.2, The Strength of Weak Ties|See why acquaintances can connect people to information outside densely connected close-friend circles.|local:catalog:weak-ties|Same weak-tie information-access mechanism as the earlier card.|

Triadic closure|idea|idea|ties|§3.1|Understand why two people sharing a friend are more likely to form a connection, without treating this as inevitable.|Q2715623|A network-formation tendency is more specific than the general network representation.|

Local bridge in a network|idea|idea|ties|§3.2, Bridges and Local Bridges|Identify a tie whose endpoints have no mutual neighbor and whose removal makes their shortest connecting path longer.|local:catalog:structural-holes|A precise edge property differs from the broader brokerage gap between social groups.|Local bridge

Structural holes|idea|idea|ties|§3.5, Structural holes|Recognize opportunities for brokerage where otherwise weakly connected groups hold different information.|local:catalog:structural-holes|Same supported brokerage meaning as the prior candidate; preserve canonical ID.|Structural hole

Betweenness centrality|idea|idea|ties|§3.6, betweenness measures|Measure how much shortest-path traffic passes through a node or edge rather than simply counting its immediate contacts.|Q5062194|This is one specific path-based centrality measure, distinct from general centrality and eigenvector centrality.|

Strong triadic closure property|facet_or_application|idea|ties|§3.2, Strong Triadic Closure Property|Use an explicitly idealized rule that two strong neighbors must also have some tie to derive network consequences.|Q2715623|A formal conditional modeling assumption is distinct from the empirical tendency of triadic closure; the source warns it is too strong universally.|

Edge embeddedness|idea|idea|ties|§3.5, Embeddedness|Count the mutual neighbors of a connected pair to describe the social context surrounding their tie.|local:catalog:structural-holes|A quantitative local-overlap measure differs from the gap and brokerage opportunity represented by structural holes.|

Structural balance in social networks|idea|idea|balance|§5.1, Structural Balance|Model consistency of positive and negative ties by distinguishing balanced triangles from potentially conflicting configurations.|Q2715623|This signed-triad model is a particular theory of relationships, not social networks generally.|Structural balance

Signed social network|idea|idea|balance|Chapter 5 introduction; §5.1|Represent both friendly and antagonistic relations with edge signs instead of recording only whether a relationship exists.|Q2715623|Adding the valence of ties yields a defined representational extension, distinct from a theory of balanced triangles.|Signed network

Dyad (social group)|idea|idea|groupsize|§6.2, Dyads, Triads, and Large Groups|See why a two-person group depends on both members' continued participation and cannot outlast either member's departure.|Q2715623|A two-member interaction structure is a specific social group form, not a general network.|Dyad

Triad (social group)|idea|idea|groupsize|§6.2, Dyads, Triads, and Large Groups|See how adding a third member permits coalitions and lets the group persist after one member leaves.|Q2715623|A three-person social group differs from a musical chord, abstract triangle, and two-member dyad.|Triad

Reference groups|idea|idea|grouptypes|§6.1, Reference Groups|Distinguish groups used as comparison standards from groups someone actually joins.|local:catalog:reference-groups|Same comparative-standard meaning already represented by the baseline.|Reference group

Social norms|idea|idea|norms|§3.2, Norms|Recognize shared expectations for conduct, including unwritten rules learned by observing others and their consequences.|Q21201|A behavioral expectation is a specific social mechanism rather than the field of sociology.|Social norm

Institutionalization|idea|idea|socialreality|§4.3, school example|Understand how shared conventions become established social institutions that outlast the original participants.|Q43229|Establishing a convention as a durable social institution differs from an organization as a purposive entity.|

Ascribed status|idea|idea|socialreality|§4.3, Roles and Status|Identify social positions assigned without personal choice and the expectations attached to them.|local:catalog:role-conflict|A category of social position differs from conflict between the roles associated with positions.|

Achieved status|idea|idea|socialreality|§4.3, Roles and Status|Identify social positions acquired through activity or choice, while separating the position from its expected behaviors.|local:catalog:role-conflict|The way a status is acquired differs from the incompatibility of role demands.|

Role-set|idea|idea|socialreality|§4.3, Roles and Status, Merton paragraph|Recognize that one social status can carry several distinct role relationships and expectations.|local:catalog:role-strain|A collection of roles attached to a status is a structure; strain is the difficulty arising from demands within a role.|Role set

Role conflict|idea|idea|socialreality|§4.3, Roles and Status, parent-worker example|Distinguish incompatible obligations between different roles from excessive demands within one role.|local:catalog:role-conflict|Same cross-role incompatibility meaning as the baseline control.|

Role strain|idea|idea|socialreality|§4.3, Roles and Status, parenting example|Recognize competing or excessive demands within a single role even without a clash between separate roles.|local:catalog:role-strain|Same within-role pressure meaning already represented in the baseline.|

Collective behavior|topic|idea|collective|§21.1, Forms of Collective Behavior|Study noninstitutionalized group activity while distinguishing a shared gathering from a formally regulated organization.|Q21201|A class of loosely organized group activity is narrower than sociology generally.|

Emergent norm theory|idea|idea|collective|§21.1, Emergent-Norm Perspective|Explain crowd conduct through locally developing guidelines in unfamiliar situations rather than assuming all crowds act irrationally.|Q21201|This theory focuses on norm development; it differs from merely naming collective behavior.|

Value-added theory of collective behavior|idea|idea|collective|§21.1, Value-Added Theory|Analyze several proposed conditions for collective episodes, including strain, shared beliefs, and precipitating events.|Q186531|This sociological explanatory model differs from philosophical value theory and accounting value added.|Value-added theory

Assembling perspective|idea|idea|collective|§21.1, Assembling Perspective|Examine how gatherings form and act through observable component processes instead of treating a crowd as one mind.|Q21201|A process-focused framework differs from emergent-norm and prerequisite-condition accounts of collective behavior.|

Resource mobilization theory|idea|idea|movements|§21.2, Resource Mobilization|Explain collective organizing partly through acquiring time, money, and people rather than grievances alone.|Q43229|This account of movement capacity differs from organizations generally and from psychological motivation.|Resource mobilization

Frame alignment|idea|idea|movements|§21.2, Framing/Frame Analysis|Connect a movement's interpretations and goals with prospective participants or allied groups to support coordinated action.|Q5164487|Constructive alignment is instructional design; frame alignment connects social-movement interpretations and audiences.|

Conversational turn-taking|idea|idea|turnanticipation|Introduction; Abstract and experiment summary|Coordinate alternating speakers partly by anticipating possible turn endings rather than waiting only to react after silence.|Q11024|Temporal allocation of conversational speaking differs from communication generally.|Turn-taking

Transition-relevance place|facet_or_application|idea|turnanticipation|Introduction, turn-constructional units and allocation rules|Recognize a possible completion point where another speaker may take over, although the current speaker can continue.|Q11024|A possible transition point is a structural component of turn-taking, not every actual end or pause.|Transition relevance place;TRP

Adjacency pair|idea|idea|grounding|Evidence in Grounding, printed p. 132|See how an initial conversational action makes a specific kind of response relevant, such as an answer after a question.|Q11024|Sequential action relevance differs from a mere pair of adjacent sentences or graph adjacency.|

Other-initiated conversational repair|idea|idea|repair|Introduction; Materials and Methods, repair-sequence definition|Signal trouble with another speaker's message so the original speaker can repeat, clarify, or confirm it.|Q11024|A collaborative breakdown-repair mechanism differs from communication generally and from repairing physical objects.|Other-initiated repair

Open repair request|facet_or_application|idea|repair|Results, Three basic types recur in all languages, pp. 4–5|Request help with an unclear message without specifying which part caused difficulty.|Q11024|An unrestricted trouble signal differs from requests targeting a particular component and from proposing a candidate interpretation.|

Restricted repair request|facet_or_application|idea|repair|Results, Three basic types recur in all languages, pp. 4–5|Target a specific missing or unclear component so the original speaker can give a focused clarification.|Q11024|Identifying the troublesome slot differs from an open request and from offering an answer for confirmation.|

Candidate-understanding repair|facet_or_application|idea|repair|Results, restricted offer definition and response patterns, pp. 4–5|Offer a possible interpretation of the prior message and ask the original speaker to confirm or correct it.|Q11024|A restricted offer supplies a candidate solution; a restricted request only identifies what needs explanation.|Restricted repair offer;Candidate understanding

Grounding in communication|idea|idea|grounding|Opening; Grounding in Conversation; contribution model|Establish mutual evidence that a message is understood well enough for the participants' current purpose.|Q11024|Grounding is the collaborative acceptance process within communication, not transmission alone.|

Common ground in communication|idea|idea|grounding|Opening definition, printed p. 127|Use mutually taken-for-granted knowledge, beliefs, and assumptions as the shared basis for coordinated communication.|Q9081|Mutually recognized shared information differs from knowledge held by one individual or facts that merely happen to overlap.|Common ground

Conversational acknowledgment|idea|idea|grounding|Evidence in Grounding, printed pp. 131–132|Provide brief verbal or gestural evidence of understanding, often without taking over the speaking turn.|Q11024|A particular feedback action differs from the overall grounding process or a full response turn.|Backchannel;Acknowledgment

Least collaborative effort|idea|idea|grounding|Least Collaborative Effort, printed p. 134|Model conversational choices by the combined work of both participants through mutual acceptance, rather than minimizing only speaking effort.|Q11024|A proposed joint-effort principle is distinct from communication generally and from making every utterance maximally complete.|

Reviewability of communication|facet_or_application|idea|grounding|Grounding Changes with the Medium, constraint 7|Use persistent messages that an addressee can revisit, changing the need and cost of repetition during coordination.|Q11024|The ability to inspect prior messages differs from the sender's ability to revise them before sending.|Reviewability

Impression management|idea|idea|socialreality|§4.3, Goffman's role performance and courtroom props|Shape how others interpret a social performance through behavior, setting, and visible cues.|Q21201|An interactional presentation mechanism differs from sociology generally and from a research subject trying to satisfy an experimenter.|
